t.6.114.2: Ah, how true and auspicious this popular saying seems to me: joy comes to a man who lives on, even if only after a hundred years.
t.6.114.1: Many years indeed have passed, and now I hear the delightful tidings of my lord, who had gone away into the vast forest.
t.6.114.3: How did the meeting of Rāghava and the monkeys come about? In what place, and on what basis? Tell me this, for I am asking.
t.6.114.4: Questioned by the prince and seated upon a mat of grass, he then related all the deeds of Rāma in the forest.
t.6.114.5: How Rāma went into exile when the boon was granted to your mother, and how King Daśaratha died of grief for his son.
t.6.114.7: Having gone to Mount Citrakūṭa, you, following the dharma of the virtuous, invited your brother, the tormentor of enemies, to take up the kingdom.
t.6.114.6: How you, O lord, were swiftly brought back by the messengers from the king's palace, and how, after you had entered Ayodhyā, the kingdom was not desired by you.
t.6.114.8: How the kingdom was given up by him who stood firm in the king's word, and how you came back again, carrying the noble one's sandals.
t.6.114.9: O mighty-armed one, all this is known to you exactly as it happened; but hear from me what took place after you had gone back.
t.6.114.11: As they were going through the dense forest, the mighty Virādha appeared before them, roaring a very great roar.
t.6.114.10: Then, when you had departed, he entered the vast and desolate Daṇḍaka forest, whose deer and birds were thrown into alarm.
t.6.114.13: Having accomplished that difficult deed, the two brothers Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa went in the evening to the delightful hermitage of Śarabhaṅga.
t.6.114.12: Lifting him up as he roared mightily, his arms raised high and his face turned downward, they hurled him into the dug pit like a trumpeting elephant.
t.6.114.14: When Śarabhaṅga had attained heaven, Rāma, whose prowess was true, saluted all the sages and went to Janasthāna.
t.6.114.15: Fourteen thousand rākṣasas of terrible deeds were slain by the great-souled Rāghava while he was dwelling there.
t.6.114.16: After that, Śūrpaṇakhā came to Rāma's side; then Lakṣmaṇa, instructed by Rāma, swiftly rose up.
t.6.114.17: Seizing a sword, the mighty one cut off her ears and nose. Then, tormented by him, the young woman went to Rāvaṇa.
t.6.114.18: A dreadful rākṣasa named Mārīca, a follower of Rāvaṇa, became a deer made of jewels and lured Vaidehī.
t.6.114.19: Having seen it, Vaidehī said to Rāma, "Let it be caught! Ah, how charming and lovely it will be in our hermitage!"
t.6.114.21: Then, O gentle one, when Rāghava had gone after the deer and Lakṣmaṇa too had gone out, Daśagrīva entered the hermitage and swiftly seized Sītā, as a planet in the sky seizes Rohiṇī.
t.6.114.20: Rāma, at full stretch and bow in hand, ran after him as he fled, and he struck him down as he ran with an arrow of smooth, well-fitted joints.
t.6.114.22: Then, having slain in battle the vulture Jaṭāyus, who wished to rescue her, that Rāvaṇa forcibly seized Sītā and swiftly went away.
t.6.114.23: Then the mountain-like monkeys, wondrous in appearance and standing on a mountain's summit, were astonished as they saw there Rāvaṇa, lord of the rākṣasas, going away after seizing Sītā.
t.6.114.24: Then Rāvaṇa, who made the worlds cry out in terror, entered Laṅkā.
t.6.114.25: Having led Maithilī into a great and splendid mansion adorned all over with gold, Rāvaṇa tried to soothe her with words.
t.6.114.26: As he was returning, Kākutstha saw the vulture and was deeply distressed.
t.6.114.27: Then Rāma, having cremated the slain vulture, his father's dear friend, wandered along the Godāvarī and through the flowering stretches of forest, and in the great forest the two came upon a rākṣasa named Kabandha.
t.6.114.28: Then, at the word of Kabandha, Rāma, whose prowess is true, went to Mount Ṛśyamūka and met with Sugrīva.
t.6.114.29: Earlier, out of affection, a heartfelt meeting had taken place between the two of them; and from their conversation with one another, a deep bond of friendship grew between them.
t.6.114.30: Having slain in battle the huge-bodied and mighty Vālin, Rāma, by the strength of his own arm, restored to him his own kingdom.
t.6.114.31: Sugrīva, installed in the kingship, together with all the monkeys, pledged to Rāma the search for the king's daughter.
t.6.114.32: Commanded by the great-souled Sugrīva, lord of the monkeys, ten crores of monkeys were dispatched to all the directions.
t.6.114.34: But the mighty brother of the king of vultures, Sampāti by name, made known that Sītā was dwelling in the abode of Rāvaṇa.
t.6.114.33: For those of us who had lost our way on the Vindhya, best of mountains, and were sorely tormented by grief, a long time went by.
t.6.114.35: Then I, seeking to dispel the sorrow of her kinsmen, who were overwhelmed with grief, relied on my own strength and leapt across a hundred yojanas.
t.6.114.36: There I saw her, alone, gone into the Aśoka grove, clad in a soiled silken garment, joyless, and firm in her vow.
t.6.114.37: Having met her in due form and asked the blameless lady about everything, and having received the jewel as a token of recognition, I have returned with my purpose accomplished.
t.6.114.38: And having come back again, I gave Rāma, of tireless deeds, the token of recognition: that radiant great jewel.
t.6.114.39: Hearing of that Maithilī, he was overjoyed and began to hope for life again, like a sick man who had reached the very end of his life on drinking nectar.
t.6.114.41: Then, having reached the ocean, he had Nala build a bridge, and by that bridge the army of the heroic monkeys crossed over.
t.6.114.40: Intending to set the enterprise in motion, he fixed his mind on the destruction of Laṅkā, like Vibhāvasu, the fire, eager to destroy the worlds, all those worlds.
t.6.114.42: Nīla slew Prahasta, while Rāghava slew Kumbhakarṇa; Lakṣmaṇa slew the son of Rāvaṇa, and Rāma himself slew Rāvaṇa.
t.6.114.43: Having met with Śakra, Yama, Varuṇa and the divine sages, Kākutstha, the scorcher of foes, received boons.
t.6.114.44: He, having been graciously granted a boon and joined by the monkeys, went to Kiṣkindhā in the aerial chariot Puṣpaka.
t.6.114.45: Having reached the Gaṅgā once more, he is dwelling in the presence of the sage; tomorrow, under the conjunction of Puṣya, you shall see Rāma, unhindered.
t.6.114.46: Then Bharata, having heard those great and truthful words of Hanumān, was filled with joy, and with joined palms he spoke words that gladdened the heart: "At long last, indeed, my heart's desire is fulfilled!"
